                                            PROJECT NO. 58481



RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                             §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                          §                         OF TEXAS


     COMMENTS BY APERTURE, LLC ON STAFF’S NEW DRAFT 16 TAC §25.194

       Aperture, LLC (Aperture) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments by its
economist, Dr. August Ankum, addressing Staff’s proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code
(TAC) §25.194.

        Aperture is a consulting firm actively engaged in public utility regulation with a special
interest in data center deployments and large load issues, such as those addressed in this project.
Dr. Ankum, with a team of Aperture consultants, has monitored and participated in various
proceedings at FERC and around the country grappling with often contentious large-load-related
issues. We hereby offer these comments.1



         Draft 16 TAC §25.194 will not substantially alleviate ERCOT’s growing and
                                paralyzing grid congestion

        Texas is generally perceived as welcoming toward data center operators and offers some
of the most generous incentives in the country. For example, Texas offers a significant sales tax
exemption for qualified data centers. (https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/data-centers/) Given
other data center friendly incentives, the low cost of electricity and plenty of affordable land,
Texas is now rivalling Northern Virginia in data center deployments, stimulating the State’s
economy and placing it at the epicenter of a global battle for AI / data center dominance. The
stakes in this regard are high; some say existential.2 Unfortunately, the merits of Staff’s efforts
notwithstanding, draft 16 TAC §25.194 does not effectively address one of SB6’s overriding
concerns: growing grid congestion.

        The rapid expansion of hyperscale data centers is fundamentally transforming the
electricity sector. Driven by surging demand from artificial intelligence, cloud computing and
digital services, these facilities are seeking grid access at unprecedented scales and speeds. Often
requiring hundreds of megawatts, the loads are not merely consuming electricity. They are
reshaping infrastructure, raising reliability concerns and triggering transmission and capacity

1
         The ideas expressed herein have previously been published in Utility Dive in two related articles:
https://www.utilitydive.com/news/market-interconnection-queue-backlog-allocation-ferc/744138/ ;
https://www.utilitydive.com/news/data-center-load-growth-markets-ratepayer/749715/
2
         https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/what-america-gets-wrong-about-ai-race

                                                                                                              1
 investments that ripple across the system. These developments are true in other states, but
especially in Texas. ERCOT in its various Report on the Capacity, Demand and Reserves (CDR)
in the ERCOT Region consistently shows requests for interconnection far outstripping available
capacity. Likewise, in its Board of Directors meeting, Item 16.2: System Planning and
Weatherization Update, ERCOT noted that interconnection requests are projected to almost
double its grid capacity by 2030:

            ERCOT has received 225 new Large Load interconnection requests in 2005
            which account for a 270% MW demand increase since January.
                                                […]
            ERCOT is tracking approximately 226 GW of Large Loads seeking
            interconnection (compared to 63 GW in December 2024) of which about 73%
            are data centers. (Emphasis added.)

       Most industry observers recognize that ERCOT will not be able to accommodate this
growing demand and applicants will have to wait idly in long queues – a situation that SB6 is
intended to address:
            While the new law is intended to streamline the interconnection process for
            large loads, and thereby decrease interconnection waiting times, it also imposes
            new requirements and hurdles that will affect how developers of large loads
            design and implement their projects. 3

        To be sure, the challenge is not whether to accommodate this growth, but how to do so
without distorting electricity markets by or forcing other customers to subsidize private
infrastructure. In a system already strained by resource constraints and planning delays, adding
large, concentrated loads without clear price signals risks driving costly misallocations and
undermining the very markets that support long-term reliability and investment.

       As the framers of SB6 recognized, the situation is urgent. Load growth on this scale,
nationwide but especially in Texas, is no longer theoretical. It is happening now, and electricity
markets must adapt, starting with a more disciplined and transparent approach to how grid
access should be priced and allocated.



            Quantity rationing by institutional responses - such as those in Draft 16 TAC
                                §25.194 – will be inadequate

      For years, interconnection reform has been framed as a process challenge rather than an
economic one. The prevailing view assumes that speculation in interconnection queues is an

3
        https://www.bracewell.com/resources/texas-senate-bill-6-ushers-in-major-overhaul-of-large-load-
interconnection-and-grid-access-rules/

                                                                                                          2
 administrative inefficiency, an unfortunate but fixable consequence of outdated procedures. The
proposed solutions follow that logic: more standardization, stricter readiness requirements and
incremental rule changes like milestone payments. That approach misses the point. The real issue
is not queue management. It is mispricing.
         The interconnection queue is, at its core, a rationing mechanism for access to limited
transmission capacity. But unlike other scarce resources in a market economy, interconnection
access is not priced according to supply and demand. Instead, it is assigned through a first-come,
first-served system that encourages gaming and speculation: quantity rationing.

       Historically, load interconnection was handled discreetly between large customers,
ERCOT and local utilities. But the size and concentration of today's hyperscale loads, often co-
located in clusters and dependent on transmission-scale delivery, demand broader scrutiny.
Regional transmission organizations and regulators are being pulled into these discussions,
especially when grid reliability and cost allocation are at stake.

         In a prominent case, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in November
2024, rejected an amended interconnection service agreement (ISA) involving PJM, Talen’s
Susquehanna Nuclear and a co-located Amazon (AWS) data center. The ISA sought to increase
load at the nuclear facility by nearly 200 MW, but ultimately to 960 MW. A separate agreement
between Talen and AWS planned to raise capacity ultimately to 1920 MW. FERC's decision
reflected concern that PJM had not adequately justified deviations from its standard open access
tariff (OAT) nor addressed broader implications for system reliability and fairness. The ruling
highlights the growing complexity of integrating large, transmission-scale loads and the inability
of current frameworks to handle them. As the Commission knows, FERC has just recently taken
comments on a Large Load Notice of Proposed Rule Making. Many other states have or are
working on large load rules comparable to Draft 16 TAC §25.194, although the thresholds for
large loads are much lower than SB6’s 75 MW, and more typically 20-25 MW.

        In all states, the situation is urgent and the challenges are real. But in most states, as in
Texas, the response so far has leaned toward tweaking institutional rules with administrative
discretion creating a case-by-case patchwork. This approach will prove inadequate. In fact, it
mirrors what renowned Harvard Professor William Hogan warned against for decades: market
distortions when scarce resources are allocated by rules and negotiations rather than prices.

        History and economics have shown uncontrovertibly, markets are superior to well-
intended but complex regulations in allocating scarce resources. It is time to remind ourselves of
this proven truth. To address grid congestion, grid access must be allocated - auctioned - based
on market principles.




                                                                                                        3
                                      Grid capacity is not free

        The transmission grid is finite and valuable. It is limited by geography, timing and
technical constraints. If a 500-MW data center requests interconnection in a congested zone, it
does not merely tap into excess supply. It displaces other users and drives the need for new
infrastructure. That demand imposes a real opportunity cost that should be taken into
consideration. And ignoring those costs is economically indefensible. It violates the principle of
cost causality that underpins utility regulation and market design. More importantly, it dulls the
investment signals that should guide where and how the system expands. If we want an optimal
allocation of grid access and, commensurately, grid investments to flow where they are needed
most, we need price signals that reflect scarcity.



                                  Pricing the scarcity - Auctions

        So what is the right solution? Consistent with economic theory, the most efficient one
should reflect marginal cost: i.e., pricing access in line with the actual impact each project has on
the grid. In areas of the grid where there is sufficient headroom and no risk of congestion, access
can and should be inexpensive or free. When grid upgrades are required to accommodate a new
load, the costs of those upgrades should be paid by the entity that caused them. And in areas
where capacity is scarce and highly valued, access should be allocated through market-based
mechanisms that reflect what users are willing to pay.

        This pricing structure could take many forms: auction-based access rights, location-
specific pricing, or forward capacity markets for transmission, and importantly, tradable queue
positions. Rather than treating queue positions as fixed administrative assignments, queue
positions should be transferable. A market for queue positions would ensure that access goes to
those who value it most, reducing congestion and improving efficiency. Again, markets – not
regulators – should decide which projects are most valuable.

        The form may vary by region, but the function must be the same: to reveal scarcity,
reward efficient siting, and ensure those driving new demand also fund the infrastructure needed
to serve it.

        This is not about blocking data centers – far from it. It is about enabling them to grow
efficiently, without placing the financial burden of their development on the broader public.
Hyperscale loads are welcome, but they should pay the full incremental cost of the capacity they
consume. If they choose to locate in constrained areas, they should cover the incremental
infrastructure costs. If they want lower-cost access, they should consider siting in areas where
transmission capacity already exists or investing in on-site or behind-the-meter resources to
reduce their impact.



                                                                                                    4
         Some argue these costs should be socialized in the name of job creation, local tax
revenues, or innovation. But every infrastructure investment has both benefits and costs. The
electricity system should not function as a hidden subsidy mechanism for large, well-capitalized
private developers. If costs are socialized while profits remain private, the result is an unjust and
economically inefficient allocation of resources.



                            Lessons from the FCC spectrum auction
        Starting in the 1990s, the Federal Communications Commission spectrum auction
transformed wireless spectrum allocation. Prior to its introduction, spectrum was assigned
administratively, leading to inefficiencies and underutilization. Competitive bidding forced
spectrum to be allocated to those who valued it most, vastly improving overall efficiency.

       Interconnection capacity should be treated the same way. It is a scarce, high-value
resource that should be priced accordingly. If concerns over market power exist, they should be
addressed through well designed auction rules, not by preserving an inefficient administrative
process.



                         Avoiding the trap of administrative discretion

        Today's interconnection processes, in Texas and elsewhere, were not designed for this
scale of load growth. They were built for generators and rely on queuing logic and engineering
studies to manage access. These processes never did reflect the economic value of grid capacity.
As a result, access to the system is being rationed on a McDonald’s style first-come, first-served
basis - by order in line, not by the value a project creates or its willingness to fund upgrades.

        This creates hidden inefficiencies. Higher-value projects can be stuck behind lower-value
ones. Load that would be willing to pay for access is sidelined by procedural rules. And political
discretion creeps into the process as policymakers and utilities decide who gets expedited
treatment and who waits. These are not market outcomes. They are administrative workarounds
to a broken allocation model.



                                  Grid access - the path forward

        Grid access must be treated like energy and capacity: as a scarce, priced product. That
means building markets for interconnection capacity, moving away from socialized costs and
reinforcing the principle that those who impose system costs must be the ones to bear them.

       The foundational market structures already exist exist in ERCOT. Energy is priced at the
margin. Congestion is hedged through financial transmission rights. Capacity is auctioned. What

                                                                                                     5
 remains is to extend that same logic to the “right” to physically connect new demand to the
system: auctioning grid access rights. When demand for interconnection exceeds available
capacity, access should be awarded through competitive bidding. If markets are efficient,
competitive bidding will drive access to reflect a proper balance between marginal benefits and
marginals costs. This is the very definition of economic efficiency.

        Hyperscale data center growth will not slow down. Nor should it. But if data centers are
to grow at scale, they must operate within a framework that respects the economic and physical
limits of the grid. The electricity system does not need new barriers. It needs clear, fair and
market disciplined market rules that are economically efficient.

        Markets work. But only when prices reflect scarcity. If we ignore that truth in the name of
expediency or growth, we will misallocate billions in infrastructure investment, erode public
trust and compromise the long-term reliability and fairness of the system.
        While some may perceive these comments to be beyond the Staff defined scope of the
Draft 16 TAC §25.194, they are not. They go to the essence of the problem SB6 is intended to
address. Getting it right is not just about powering data centers. It is about preserving the
integrity of electricity markets, ensuring affordable, reliable power for everyone and, ultimately,
economic efficiency. Let markets work.



                                            Conclusion

        Aperture appreciates this opportunity to provide comment on Draft 16 TAC §25.194, and
looks forward to working with Staff, the Commission, ERCOT and other stakeholders to best
manage grid congestion and ensure that Texas continues to be in the lead in data center
deployments.


Respectfully submitted,

   August Ankum, Ph.D.
   Senior Vice President
   Aperture, LLC

                                     Executive Summary
       These comments do not address specific subsections but rather the overall approach to
SB6’s intentions. We argue that notwithstanding the merits of Staff’s efforts, Staff’s new Draft 16
TAC §25.194 does not effectively address one of SB6’s overriding concerns: growing grid
congestion.

The problem:

      Most industry observers recognize that ERCOT will not be able to accommodate
       explosive demand for interconnection and applicants will have to wait idly in long
       queues. As the framers of SB6 recognized, the situation is urgent and electricity markets
       must adapt. But the proposed draft solutions follow the faulty logic of more
       standardization, stricter readiness requirements and incremental rule changes. That
       approach, however, misses the point. The real issue is not queue management. It is
       mispricing.
      The interconnection queue is, at its core, a rationing mechanism for access to limited
       transmission capacity. The problem is that unlike other scarce resources in a market
       economy, interconnection access is not priced according to supply and demand. Rather, it
       is assigned through a first-come, first-served system that encourages gaming and
       speculation: i.e., rationing, which by definition is equivalent to ever longer queues.

The solution:

      Grid access must be treated like energy and capacity: as a scarce, priced product. That
       means building markets for interconnection capacity. The foundational structures already
       exist in ERCOT. Energy is priced at the margin. Congestion is hedged through financial
       transmission rights. Capacity is auctioned. What remains is to extend that same logic to
       the “right” to physically connect new demand to the system: auctioning grid access
       rights. When demand for interconnection exceeds available capacity, access should be
       awarded through competitive bidding, as the FCC did in the 1990s with its spectrum
       auctions. If markets are efficient, competitive bidding will drive access to reflect a
       proper balance between marginal benefits and marginals costs. This is the very definition
       of economic efficiency.
      Hyperscale data center growth will not slow down. Nor should it. But if data centers are
       to grow at scale, they must operate within a framework that respects the economic and
       physical limits of the grid. The electricity system does not need new barriers. It needs
       clear, fair and market disciplined market rules that are economically efficient and provide
       proper incentives for capacity expansions.
      Markets work. But only when prices reflect scarcity. If we ignore that truth in the name of
       expediency or growth, we will misallocate billions in infrastructure investment, erode
       public trust and compromise the long-term reliability and fairness of the system.

The solution:

   •   Grid access must be treated like energy and capacity: as a scarce, priced product. That
       means building markets for interconnection capacity. The foundational structures already
       exist in ERCOT. Energy is priced at the margin. Congestion is hedged through financial
       transmission rights. Capacity is auctioned. What remains is to extend that same logic to
       the "righf' to physically connect new demand to the system: auctioning grid access
       dghts. When demand for interconnection exceeds available capacitv, access should be
       awarded through competitive bidding, as the FCC did in the 1990s with its spectrum
       auctions- If markets are efficient, competitive bidding will drive access to reflect a
       proper balance between marginal benefits and marginals costs. This is the very definition
       of economic efficiency.
   •   Hyperscale data center growth will not slow down. Nor should it. But if data centers are
       to grow at scale, they must operate within a framework that respects the economic and
       physical limits of the grid. The electricity system does not need new barriers. It needs
       clear, fair and market disciplined market rules that are economically efficient and provide
       proper incentives for capacity expansions.
   •   Markets work. But only when prices reflect scarcity. If we ignore that truth in the name of
       expediency or growth, we will misallocate billions in infrastructure investment, erode
       public trust and compromise the long-term reliability and fairness of the system.
